chapters.title: First Steps

tasks.label: run help to see all commands

chapters.funFact: a shell is just a loop: read input, find the program, run it, print the output. every terminal since 1971 works this way.

chapters.title: Look Around

tasks.label: find out where you are with pwd

chapters.funFact: pwd stands for 'print working directory'. it tells you exactly where you are in the filesystem tree, like gps for your terminal.

chapters.title: Read Files
chapters.funFact: cat is short for concatenate. it was built to join files together, but became the universal 'just show me the file' command. ken thompson wrote it in 1971.

chapters.title: Navigate
hints: try: pwd then cd (with no arguments goes home)
chapters.funFact: unix paths use / as a separator because the original pdp-7 keyboard didn't have a backslash key. windows later chose \\ to be different.

chapters.title: Hidden Files
chapters.funFact: files starting with a dot are hidden in unix. this was actually a bug in the original ls that checked for . and .. but accidentally hid all dotfiles. the bug became a feature.

chapters.title: Directory Tree

tasks.label: view the root filesystem with tree /

chapters.funFact: a real linux system has hundreds of thousands of files. underneath, every file is just a number (an inode) in a flat table on disk.

chapters.title: System Config
chapters.funFact: /etc/passwd dates back to the 1970s. modern systems store actual password hashes in /etc/shadow, which only root can read.

chapters.title: System Logs
chapters.funFact: every time linux boots, the kernel logs what it found: hardware, drivers, filesystems. sysadmins read these logs when something breaks at 3am.

chapters.title: Temp Files
chapters.funFact: /tmp is world-writable (permission 1777). the sticky bit means anyone can create files, but only the owner can delete them.

chapters.title: Your Projects
hints: try: cat followed by any .md file (use tab)
chapters.funFact: these .md files were fetched from the github api. the filesystem is virtual, running in webassembly, but behaves exactly like a real one.

chapters.title: Project Commands
hints: try: readme reponame, open reponame, then cd
chapters.funFact: these commands hit the github api in real time. the project command is like man pages: a concept from 1971 where every unix tool had a manual.

chapters.title: Identity
chapters.funFact: whoami was added to unix in the 1970s. in multi-user systems with shared terminals, you genuinely might forget which account you logged into.

chapters.title: System Info
chapters.funFact: neofetch is a modern flex tool for showing system specs. uname has existed since the 1970s. the -a flag shows all system info at once.

chapters.title: Date and Time
chapters.funFact: the date command outputs iso 8601 format by default. this standard ensures dates sort correctly: year-month-day. invented in 1988 to end date format wars.

chapters.title: Create Files
chapters.funFact: touch doesn't just create files. it updates timestamps. sysadmins use it to mark when something was last checked.

chapters.title: Delete Files

tasks.label: create a test directory: mkdir testdir

hints: try: mkdir testdir then rm testdir
chapters.funFact: there is no recycle bin in unix. rm unlinks the file's inode. this is why 'rm -rf /' is the most feared command in computing.

chapters.title: Copy and Move
chapters.funFact: mv and cp are from original unix (1971). mv is actually a rename at the filesystem level unless crossing filesystems, then it copies and deletes.

chapters.title: Symbolic Links
chapters.funFact: symlinks are special files containing a path to another file. they can cross filesystems and point to directories. broken symlinks are a classic source of bugs.

chapters.title: Echo and Variables
chapters.funFact: environment variables like $HOME and $PWD are inherited by every process. $HOME was standardized in posix 1988 and exists on every unix system.

chapters.title: Command History

tasks.label: use up arrow to recall a command

hints: press up arrow to cycle through previous commands
chapters.funFact: your history is stored in ~/.zsh_history. some developers have history files with 100,000+ entries spanning years of work.

chapters.title: Pipes

tasks.label: make the cow say something colorful

chapters.funFact: pipes were invented by doug mcilroy at bell labs in 1973. the philosophy: make each program do one thing well, then connect them.

chapters.title: Output Redirection
hints: try: cat myfile.txt then echo world >> myfile.txt
chapters.funFact: unix has three standard streams: stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2). redirection rewires these at the kernel level. you can even redirect errors with 2>.

chapters.title: Command Chaining
chapters.funFact: && is the AND operator: run next only if previous succeeds. || is OR: run next only if previous fails. error handling in one character.

chapters.title: The Editor
hints: inside: i to type, Esc to stop, :wq to save and quit
chapters.funFact: vim uses modal editing: normal mode for navigation, insert mode for typing. designed in 1976 for terminals so slow that every keystroke had to count.

chapters.title: Easter Eggs

tasks.label: find the ascii art with echo $USER

chapters.funFact: sl was written in 1993 by a japanese professor to punish students who mistyped ls. sudo (superuser do) was created in 1980 so admins didn't share root passwords.

chapters.title: Multiple Arguments
chapters.funFact: cat was literally designed to concatenate files. cat file1 file2 outputs both in sequence. this is how you merge files: cat a.txt b.txt > combined.txt

chapters.title: Complex Pipelines

tasks.label: chain cd, ls, and cat in one line

chapters.funFact: you just did what sysadmins do hundreds of times a day: navigate, inspect, and transform data without leaving the keyboard.

chapters.title: Full System Info

tasks.label: print all system info with uname -a

chapters.funFact: uname -a shows kernel name, hostname, version, architecture, and more. this command exists on every unix system ever made since the 1970s.

chapters.title: Tab Completion

tasks.label: type cat ab then press tab
type cd pro then press tab

hints: type cat ab then press tab to autocomplete
type cd pro then press tab
chapters.funFact: tab completion was added to csh in 1978 by bill joy. modern shells complete commands, files, git branches, hostnames, and more. it saves thousands of keystrokes per day.

chapters.title: Graduation
chapters.funFact: training complete. you now know how to navigate, read, create, destroy, pipe, redirect, and chain commands. every command here works the same on a real linux machine.
